<reflection>
The first experiment (run_1) with S=2.0, cat=0.05, P=0.0 yielded very similar negative log-likelihood (NLL) values for many candidate mechanisms, with most NLLs clustered around -22.2 to -22.8. This indicates that the data from a single standard condition is not sufficient to discriminate among the numerous plausible mechanisms. The aim of this turn is to design an experiment that stresses a specific mechanistic difference—namely, the role of product in deactivation versus reversible inhibition—to separate product‑dependent deactivation mechanisms (e.g., M12, M17) from simple reversible mechanisms (e.g., M1, M2) and other deactivation types.
</reflection>
<hypothesis>
The leading candidate mechanisms differ critically in whether product participates in irreversible deactivation steps. Mechanisms M12 and M17 include deactivation pathways that involve product (P+cat→inactive_catP and P+catS→inactive_catSP, respectively), while others treat product only as a reversible inhibitor or ignore its effect on catalyst stability. Adding a significant initial concentration of product (P=0.5 M) will test this difference. 

For simple reversible mechanisms (M1, M2), added product slows the initial rate due to thermodynamic reversibility and lowers the final conversion by shifting the equilibrium, but the time course remains a smooth approach to the new equilibrium. For product‑deactivation mechanisms (M12, M17), the presence of product causes immediate or accelerated loss of active catalyst, leading to a more pronounced reduction in initial rate and a lower final conversion than predicted by reversible inhibition alone. For other deactivation mechanisms (e.g., M9, M11, M13–M16, M18–M20) and substrate‑inhibition mechanisms (M7), added product primarily affects reversibility; any deactivation proceeds independently of product, so the initial‑rate reduction should resemble that of reversible mechanisms, though final conversion may be further limited by deactivation. 

Thus, measuring the time course with added product will create a clear divergence: product‑deactivation mechanisms will show stronger suppression of both rate and conversion compared to reversible mechanisms, while other deactivation mechanisms will lie somewhere in between depending on their specific pathways.
</hypothesis>
